pharm: Bactericidal aminoglycoside that binds the 30S bacterial ribosomal subunit, inhibiting protein synthesis; active primarily against aerobic Gram-negative bacilli including Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
quick: 3 mg/kg/day IV/IM in 3 divided doses q8h (serious infection); up to 5 mg/kg/day for life-threatening infection, with serum level monitoring
Not applicable - given IV/IM (not absorbed orally)
Avoid - aminoglycosides can cause fetal harm including ototoxicity; use only if benefit outweighs risk
Likely compatible - minimal oral absorption by infant; poorly excreted in milk
Dose reduction / interval extension essential; reduce dose and monitor levels per CrCl
No specific adjustment - eliminated renally, not hepatically metabolized
Not applicable - IV/IM administration; no direct interaction
Serum peak (target ~4-6 mcg/mL) and trough (<2 mcg/mL); renal function (BUN, SCr, CrCl); audiometry/vestibular function
summary: Tobramycin is a parenteral aminoglycoside antibiotic used for serious Gram-negative infections including those caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Serratia, and Proteus species. It is bactericidal, inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis. Given IV or IM at 3 mg/kg/day in divided doses (up to 5 mg/kg/day in life-threatening infection), it has a narrow therapeutic index requiring serum peak/trough monitoring and dosing by body weight. Boxed warnings highlight dose- and exposure-related nephrotoxicity, irreversible auditory and reversible/irreversible vestibular ototoxicity, and potential neuromuscular blockade. Renal function, hearing, and serum levels must be monitored closely, with dose adjustment in renal impairment, the elderly, and neonates.
indications: Septicemia (neonate, child, adult) caused by P. aeruginosa, E. coli, Klebsiella sp
Lower respiratory tract infections caused by P. aeruginosa, Klebsiella sp, Enterobacter sp, Serratia sp, E. coli, S. aureus
Serious CNS infections (meningitis) caused by susceptible organisms
Intra-abdominal infections including peritonitis caused by E. coli, Klebsiella sp, Enterobacter sp
Skin, bone, and skin-structure infections caused by P. aeruginosa, Proteus sp, E. coli, Klebsiella sp, Enterobacter sp, S. aureus
Complicated and recurrent urinary tract infections caused by P. aeruginosa, Proteus sp, E. coli, Klebsiella sp, Enterobacter sp, Serratia sp, S. aureus, Providencia sp, Citrobacter sp
Serious staphylococcal infections when penicillins or less toxic drugs are contraindicated and susceptibility supports use
Pseudomonal pulmonary exacerbations in cystic fibrosis (altered PK requires direct serum level measurement)

dosage.c: Adult - serious infection, normal renal function
dosage.d: 3 mg/kg/day in 3 equal doses (1 mg/kg q8h)
dosage.t: Usually 7-10 days; extend only with renal/auditory/vestibular monitoring
dosage.n: Dose by pretreatment body weight; use ideal body weight in obesity. Measure peak and trough serum levels.

dosage.d: Up to 5 mg/kg/day in 3 or 4 equal doses; reduce to 3 mg/kg/day as soon as clinically indicated
dosage.n: Do not exceed 5 mg/kg/day unless serum levels are monitored. Avoid prolonged levels >12 mcg/mL.

dosage.d: 6 to 7.5 mg/kg/day in 3-4 divided doses (2-2.5 mg/kg q8h or 1.5-1.89 mg/kg q6h)
dosage.t: Limit to short term; monitor with prolonged therapy

dosage.c: Neonate (premature or full-term, <=1 week of age)
dosage.d: Up to 4 mg/kg/day in 2 equal doses every 12 hours
dosage.n: Use caution due to renal immaturity and prolonged serum half-life.

dosage.d: Initial 10 mg/kg/day in 4 equally divided doses (guide only)
dosage.n: Altered PK lowers serum levels; measure serum concentrations directly to guide dosing due to wide interpatient variability.

dosage.d: Loading dose 1 mg/kg, then reduce subsequent doses and/or extend interval based on CrCl and serum levels
dosage.t: Per clinical response and serum levels
dosage.n: Monitor serum tobramycin concentrations throughout therapy; obtain levels after 2-3 doses and every 3-4 days.

admin: IV: dilute in compatible diluent and infuse over approximately 20 to 60 minutes (commonly over 30-60 min).
IM and IV dosages are identical.
Do not physically premix tobramycin with other drugs, especially beta-lactams (penicillins/cephalosporins) which can inactivate aminoglycosides in vitro; administer separately.
Draw peak level ~30 minutes after the end of an IV infusion (or 1 hour after an IM dose); draw trough just before the next dose.
Ensure adequate hydration before and during therapy to reduce nephrotoxicity risk.
Obtain pretreatment body weight to calculate the correct dose; use ideal body weight in obesity.
Pharmacy bulk package is for preparing IV admixtures only - not for direct patient administration.
Product contains sodium metabisulfite - use caution in sulfite-sensitive (especially asthmatic) patients.
moa: Tobramycin is a bactericidal aminoglycoside that diffuses across the bacterial outer membrane and is actively transported (oxygen-dependent) into the cell, where it binds irreversibly to the 30S ribosomal subunit. This impairs initiation of protein synthesis, causes misreading of mRNA, and leads to production of nonfunctional proteins and disruption of the cytoplasmic membrane, resulting in rapid concentration-dependent bacterial killing. Activity is greatest against aerobic Gram-negative bacilli; anaerobes are intrinsically resistant due to lack of oxygen-dependent uptake.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to tobramycin or any aminoglycoside (cross-sensitivity within the class is well established)
History of serious toxic reaction to any aminoglycoside
relative: Pre-existing renal impairment (requires dose adjustment and close monitoring)
Pre-existing hearing loss or vestibular dysfunction
Neuromuscular disorders (myasthenia gravis, parkinsonism) - risk of neuromuscular blockade
Known maternal history of aminoglycoside ototoxicity or MT-RNR1 (m.1555A>G) mitochondrial variant - consider alternatives
monitor: Serum peak and trough tobramycin concentrations
Renal function (BUN, serum creatinine, creatinine clearance, urinalysis)
Auditory function (serial audiograms in at-risk patients) and vestibular function
Serum calcium, magnesium, sodium, and potassium
Signs of neuromuscular blockade, particularly with anesthesia or neuromuscular blocking agents

preg: Aminoglycosides can cause fetal harm when administered to a pregnant woman; tobramycin crosses the placenta and other aminoglycosides have caused irreversible bilateral congenital deafness in children exposed in utero. Use during pregnancy only when the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus, and counsel the patient on the potential hazard.
lact: Tobramycin is poorly absorbed from the infant gastrointestinal tract, and excretion into breast milk is low; clinically significant systemic exposure in a breastfed infant is unlikely. Consider monitoring the infant for gastrointestinal effects (e.g., diarrhea, thrush). Decide whether to discontinue nursing or the drug based on the importance of the drug to the mother.
renal: Tobramycin is eliminated almost entirely by glomerular filtration, and serum half-life is inversely related to creatinine clearance. Renal impairment causes drug accumulation and increased risk of nephro- and ototoxicity. Give a loading dose of 1 mg/kg, then reduce the maintenance dose and/or extend the dosing interval according to creatinine clearance and serum levels. Monitor serum concentrations closely (after 2-3 doses and every 3-4 days, or more often with changing renal function). Tobramycin itself is nephrotoxic; nephrotoxicity is usually reversible. In dialysis patients, 25%-70% of a dose may be removed depending on the modality and duration.
hepatic: Tobramycin undergoes little or no hepatic metabolism and is eliminated unchanged by the kidneys, so no dose adjustment is needed for hepatic impairment. Reversible elevations in serum transaminases (SGOT/SGPT), LDH, and bilirubin have been reported and warrant monitoring during therapy.

major: Other neuro-/nephrotoxic antibiotics, especially other aminoglycosides (amikacin, gentamicin, streptomycin, neomycin, kanamycin, paromomycin), and cephaloridine, viomycin, polymyxin B, colistin, cisplatin, vancomycin - additive nephro-/ototoxicity; avoid concurrent or sequential use
Potent loop diuretics (ethacrynic acid, furosemide) - enhanced ototoxicity; avoid concurrent use
Neuromuscular blocking agents (succinylcholine, tubocurarine, decamethonium) and anesthetics - potentiated neuromuscular blockade and respiratory paralysis
Massive transfusion of citrated blood - may potentiate neuromuscular blockade
moderate: Cephalosporins - increased incidence of nephrotoxicity reported with concomitant use
NSAIDs (e.g., indomethacin in neonates) - reduced renal clearance and higher aminoglycoside levels
Other nephrotoxic agents (amphotericin B, contrast media) - additive renal injury
minor: Beta-lactam antibiotics - physical/chemical inactivation if mixed in the same solution (separate administration avoids the interaction; synergy is therapeutically useful when given separately)
interactions.food: Not applicable - administered parenterally; not absorbed from the GI tract.
interactions.alcohol: No clinically significant direct interaction; relevant only if alcohol-related volume depletion increases nephrotoxicity risk.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause decreased serum calcium, magnesium, sodium, and potassium and increased BUN/creatinine, transaminases, LDH, and bilirubin; can produce leukopenia, leukocytosis, eosinophilia, anemia, granulocytopenia, and thrombocytopenia. Neuromuscular blockade from tobramycin may be reversed with calcium salts.

common: Transient elevations in serum transaminases, LDH, and bilirubin
Electrolyte changes (decreased calcium, magnesium, sodium, potassium)
serious: Nephrotoxicity (rising BUN/serum creatinine, oliguria, cylindruria, proteinuria) - usually reversible
Auditory ototoxicity - tinnitus, roaring in ears, hearing loss; high-tone loss first, often irreversible and bilateral
Hematologic effects - anemia, granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia
rare: Anaphylaxis and serious allergic reactions (including from sulfite content)
Severe cutaneous reactions - exfoliative dermatitis, toxic epidermal necrolysis, erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (rarely fatal)
Ototoxicity in patients with MT-RNR1 mitochondrial variants even at therapeutic serum levels
emergency: Anaphylaxis / severe hypersensitivity - stop drug, give epinephrine and supportive care
Respiratory paralysis from neuromuscular blockade - secure airway, ventilate, give calcium salts
Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis - discontinue and provide urgent supportive care
Sudden or progressive hearing loss / vertigo - discontinue or adjust dose immediately
Severe C. difficile colitis (fulminant diarrhea, signs of toxic megacolon)

monitoring: Serum peak (drawn ~30 min after IV infusion / 1 hr after IM) target approximately 4-6 mcg/mL; avoid prolonged levels >12 mcg/mL
Serum trough (drawn just before next dose) - keep <2 mcg/mL; rising trough suggests tissue accumulation
Obtain serum assays after 2-3 doses and at 3-4 day intervals; more frequently with changing renal function
Renal function: BUN, serum creatinine, creatinine clearance, and urinalysis (specific gravity, protein, cells, casts)
Serial audiograms in at-risk patients old enough to be tested; assess vestibular function
Serum calcium, magnesium, sodium, and potassium
Hydration status and signs of neuromuscular weakness
Bacterial cultures and susceptibility before and during therapy
counsel: Report any hearing changes, ringing in the ears, dizziness, or balance problems immediately - hearing loss may be permanent and can appear after the drug is stopped.
Report decreased urination, swelling, or other signs of kidney problems.
Report severe or watery/bloody diarrhea, which may occur during or up to 2 months after treatment (possible C. difficile).
Report rash, blistering, mouth sores, or difficulty breathing - signs of a serious allergic or skin reaction.
Blood tests to measure drug levels and kidney function are required during treatment.
Inform your clinician of any family history of hearing loss with antibiotics, kidney disease, or muscle disorders such as myasthenia gravis.
Tell your clinician if you are pregnant or planning pregnancy - this drug can harm a developing baby's hearing.
Complete the full prescribed course; stopping early can promote resistant bacteria.
pk: Rapid bactericidal activity; therapeutic serum levels achieved within minutes to ~30-90 min of dosing
30-90 min after IM (similar after 1-hr IV infusion); ~4 mcg/mL after 1 mg/kg IM
~2 hours with normal renal function; prolonged (inversely with CrCl) in renal impairment and neonates
Measurable serum levels persist up to ~8 hours after a dose; dosing q8h in normal renal function
Store at 20-25 degrees C (68-77 degrees F), USP controlled room temperature
pearls: Aminoglycosides are concentration-dependent killers with a post-antibiotic effect; high peak-to-MIC ratios drive efficacy while elevated troughs drive toxicity.
Dose by ideal (lean) body weight, not total body weight, in obese patients to avoid overdosing.
Practically no protein binding and minimal hepatic metabolism - clearance tracks creatinine clearance closely.
Tobramycin is generally more active than gentamicin against P. aeruginosa and may be modestly less nephrotoxic in some studies.
Synergistic with beta-lactams against Gram-negatives and enterococci, but never mix in the same syringe/bag (in vitro inactivation).
Poor CNS/CSF penetration and minimal biliary excretion; high concentrations accumulate in renal cortex.
Inactive against anaerobes due to oxygen-dependent uptake.
Consider MT-RNR1 mitochondrial variant testing / alternatives if there is a maternal family history of aminoglycoside-associated deafness.
missed: For scheduled dosing, give the missed dose as soon as it is recognized and adjust the remaining schedule to maintain appropriate intervals; do not double doses. Because tobramycin is administered and timed by clinical staff with serum-level monitoring, a missed or delayed dose should prompt re-evaluation of the dosing schedule and may require re-checking serum levels before the next dose, especially in renal impairment.
overdose: Toxicity correlates with total exposure (AUC) and is more likely with therapy >10 days, doses >5 mg/kg/day (adults) or >7.5 mg/kg/day (children), troughs that fail to fall below 2 mcg/mL, renal impairment, dehydration, advanced age, or concurrent nephro-/ototoxic drugs. Manifestations include nephrotoxicity (acute tubular necrosis), auditory and vestibular toxicity (which may appear or progress after discontinuation), and neuromuscular blockade with possible respiratory paralysis (greatest in myasthenia gravis/Parkinson disease or with neuromuscular blockers). Management: contact a Poison Control Center; secure the airway, ensure oxygenation/ventilation, and treat respiratory paralysis promptly (calcium salts reverse neuromuscular blockade, mechanical ventilation as needed). In patients with normal renal function, hydrate to maintain urine output of 3-5 mL/kg/hr; monitor fluid balance, creatinine clearance, and plasma levels until tobramycin falls below 2 mcg/mL. Hemodialysis may be beneficial when the half-life is prolonged or renal function is abnormal.
